title: The history of GPS
tagline: From a radio beep from Sputnik to a sky of more than a hundred navigation satellites that tells your phone where it is.
intro: In 1957 two American physicists listened to the first satellite and found they could track it from the pitch of its radio signal. A colleague then asked the question that started satellite navigation: could the trick run backwards? It took clocks in orbit, a hard decision in the Pentagon, and a lot of careful maths about the shape of the Earth to turn that idea into GPS. Then the sky filled up with rival systems from Russia, Europe, China, India and Japan. Where sources disagree on a date or a number, this history says so.

eras.name: Listening to the first satellites
eras.summary: Sputnik's beep shows that a satellite can be tracked from the ground. The Navy's Transit system turns the idea around and uses satellites to fix a ship's position. Other teams start putting clocks in space.

eras.name: Building GPS
eras.summary: Navy and Air Force ideas merge into one programme called Navstar. Atomic clocks go up, the first satellite launches in 1978, and the full constellation of 24 is declared ready in 1995.

eras.name: Opening the sky to everyone
eras.summary: After a civil airliner is shot down in 1983, the US promises GPS for civil use. The deliberate blur called Selective Availability is switched off in 2000, and phones and aircraft start to rely on the signal.

eras.name: A sky of many systems
eras.summary: The Soviet Union, then Russia, builds GLONASS. Europe builds Galileo, China builds BeiDou, India builds NavIC and Japan builds QZSS. A modern phone listens to several at once.

eras.name: New signals and finer accuracy
eras.summary: A third civil signal, a new generation of satellites, and public services that promise accuracy of tens of centimetres.

events.title: Atomic clocks in orbit, on paper
events.text: The German-American physicist Friedwardt Winterberg suggested testing general relativity with accurate atomic clocks in orbit. Wikipedia dates his paper to 1955, its reference list gives 1956, and a university page quoted there says 1954.
events.why: It was an early sign that clocks in orbit would run at a different rate from clocks on the ground, which GPS later had to correct.

events.title: Sputnik beeps over the world
events.text: Sputnik 1 was a metal sphere about 58 cm wide, with a mass of about 83.6 kg (184 lb). It circled the Earth about every 96 minutes, between roughly 215 km and 939 km up. Its radio signal on about 20 and 40 MHz lasted around 22 days.
events.why: A satellite broadcasting a steady radio tone gave scientists something simple to listen to and measure.

events.title: Finding a satellite from its pitch
events.text: Two physicists at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, William Guier and George Weiffenbach, recorded Sputnik's 20 MHz radio signal. The tone they heard rose and fell as the satellite passed, because of the Doppler shift. From that curve they worked out its orbit.
events.why: A change in a signal's pitch can reveal distance and speed, which is the first step toward measuring position from space.

events.title: Turn the idea around
events.who: Frank McClure, William Guier and George Weiffenbach
events.text: On 17 March 1958 Frank McClure, head of APL's Research Center, asked Guier and Weiffenbach whether their method could be turned around: with the orbit known, could it fix a position on Earth? Their first study said yes. The Navy wanted this for Polaris submarines, and McClure and Richard Kershner outlined Transit that weekend.
events.why: It changed the question from where is the satellite to where am I.

events.title: Transit 1B reaches orbit
events.text: Transit 1A, launched on 17 September 1959, did not reach orbit. Transit 1B, launched on 13 April 1960, did, though lower than planned: about 626 km to 1,078 km.
events.why: It was the first working satellite of the first satellite navigation system.

events.title: Air Force studies Project 621B
events.who: US Air Force and The Aerospace Corporation
events.text: The Air Force backed a 1963 Aerospace Corporation study of satellite navigation, called 621B. Its ideas fed into GPS. In 1973 it was merged into the joint Navy and Air Force effort.
events.why: It was the Air Force half of what later became GPS.

events.title: Transit goes into service
events.text: Transit became fully operational in 1964. A ship fixed its position from a satellite pass, but fixes came only every 35 to 100 minutes. Early accuracy was a few hundred metres.
events.why: Transit proved the idea, and its slow, patchy coverage is what GPS was built to fix.

events.title: Timation puts a clock in orbit
events.who: Roger Easton and the Naval Research Laboratory
events.text: Timation 1 flew at 925 km with two quartz clocks, not atomic ones. Roger Easton's idea was passive ranging: a receiver measures the delay of a timed satellite signal to find its distance. He entered the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2010.
events.why: Timing, not Doppler shift, became the heart of GPS.

events.title: Transit opens to the public
events.text: In 1967 Transit was opened to private and commercial users. More than 80,000 privately owned receivers were used. Service ended on 31 December 1996.
events.why: Sailors and surveyors learned to trust satellite fixes decades before GPS.

events.title: A Labor Day weekend design session
events.text: Air Force Colonel Bradford Parkinson, named director of the new GPS joint programme office in April 1973, had about a dozen staff work out a new navigation design over Labor Day weekend 1973.
events.why: It was a turning point in shaping the design that became GPS.

events.title: Navy and Air Force merge their programmes
events.who: US Navy and US Air Force
events.text: The eoPortal Timation page says the Navy's Timation work merged with the Air Force's 621B in April 1973 to form Navstar-GPS. HISTORY says the Air Force consolidated several programmes in 1974. Parkinson and Ivan Getting later shared the 2003 Draper Prize for GPS.
events.why: Two rival ideas, Navy timing and Air Force signals, became one system.

events.title: Rubidium atomic clocks reach orbit
events.text: NTS-1 launched on 14 July 1974 into a medium orbit about 13,700 km high (one table gives 13,800 km). It was the first satellite to carry rubidium atomic clocks.
events.why: Atomic clocks in orbit were the next step toward GPS-quality timing.

events.title: Cesium clocks, and Einstein checked
events.text: NTS-2 launched on 23 June 1977 into a 20,200 km orbit with the first cesium clocks. Its clock ran faster than ground clocks by 442.5 parts in 10 to the 12, against 446.5 predicted by general relativity. Ashby reports agreement to better than 1 percent.
events.why: It showed that the relativity correction was real and that it had to be built into every GPS satellite.

events.title: The first Navstar satellite launches
events.where: Vandenberg Air Force Base, California, USA
events.text: Navstar 1 launched on 22 February 1978 from Vandenberg Air Force Base. It is described as the first operational GPS satellite. Eleven Block I satellites flew between 1978 and 1985.
events.why: The system that began as ideas on paper now had hardware in the sky.

events.title: The Soviet Union launches the first GLONASS satellite
events.text: Flight tests began on 12 October 1982 with three Kosmos satellites. GLONASS flies at about 19,100 km, in three planes of eight satellites. The full 24 was reached in 1995.
events.why: It gave the world a second global system and a fall-back for GPS.

events.title: Korean Air Lines Flight 007 is shot down
events.where: Near Moneron Island, west of Sakhalin
events.text: On 1 September 1983 a Soviet interceptor shot down Korean Air Lines Flight 007 after it strayed into Soviet airspace. All 269 people on board died.
events.why: The disaster is often given as the reason GPS was opened to civil use.

events.title: Reagan promises GPS for civil use
events.text: After the shootdown, President Reagan said the US satellite navigation system would be free for civilian use once it was working. Nextgov says he sped up the timetable. The best signals stayed reserved for the military.
events.why: Civil GPS began as a policy decision, not just a technical one.

events.title: China sketches a two-satellite system
events.text: In 1983 Chen Fangyun and colleagues proposed an experimental system built on two satellites. In February 1994 the government approved the programme, later named BeiDou.
events.why: It was the first step of the plan that led to a global BeiDou.

events.title: Gladys West shapes the Earth for GPS
events.where: Naval Proving Ground, Dahlgren, Virginia, USA
events.text: West joined the Naval Proving Ground at Dahlgren in 1956. She calculated models of the Earth's shape, including the geoid, and worked on satellite data analysis. Wikipedia adds that she programmed an IBM 7030 Stretch for this from the mid-1970s and wrote a 1986 report on GEOSAT altimeter data. Her Earth models are credited with helping GPS orbit calculations.
events.why: A satellite can only tell you where you are if its own position and the Earth's shape are known precisely.

events.title: The first Block II satellite
events.text: A Delta II rocket made its first launch on 14 February 1989, carrying the first operational Block II GPS satellite. Block II and IIA satellites were launched from 1989 to 1997, and the last was retired in 2019.
events.why: These were the workhorses that built the working constellation.

events.title: The first portable GPS for civilians
events.text: HISTORY says the Magellan Nav 1000 went on sale in 1989 as the first portable civilian GPS device, at about $3,000.
events.why: It put a satellite receiver in a hand, years before phones.

events.title: GPS goes to war before it is finished
events.text: In the 1991 Gulf War GPS was used heavily in combat, before the constellation was complete. With few military receivers available, the US bought more than 10,000 civilian ones and set Selective Availability to zero for the war.
events.why: Even a partial constellation was a big help in featureless desert.

events.title: Full operational capability
events.text: Air & Space Forces Magazine says GPS became fully operational on 27 April 1995, with 24 satellites. NASA's page dates full operation to 1993, so sources differ.
events.why: At least four satellites were now in view from almost anywhere, at any time.

events.title: The deliberate blur is switched off
events.text: At a White House briefing on 1 May 2000, officials said the US would stop deliberately degrading the public GPS signal. They said accuracy would improve from about 100 m to 10 to 20 m. GPS.gov says it took effect shortly after midnight and that the US has no intent to use it again. Sources differ on the exact hour.
events.why: Everyone's receiver became about ten times better overnight, with no new satellite.

events.title: Emergency calls pull GPS into phones
events.text: Assisted GPS sends orbit data to the phone over the mobile network. A normal receiver can need up to 12.5 minutes to collect the full message from the satellites at 50 bits per second. Wikipedia says US 911 location rules sped up its development.
events.why: It is why the blue dot on your phone appears in seconds, not minutes.

events.title: WAAS corrects GPS for pilots
events.text: An FAA spokesman told AOPA the first WAAS approach was commissioned on 10 July 2003. Wikipedia counts 38 ground stations in 2007 that measure GPS errors, with geostationary satellites sending the corrections. It reports typical accuracy better than about 1 m sideways and 1.5 m vertically.
events.why: It shows how outside help can fix errors that a lone receiver cannot see.

events.title: Europe tests Galileo in orbit
events.text: GIOVE-A, the first experimental Galileo test satellite, launched from Baikonur on 28 December 2005. Surrey Satellite Technology built it under a contract signed in July 2003. Galileo remains under civilian control.
events.why: Europe wanted a system run by civilians, not the military.

events.title: Block IIF brings a third civil signal
events.text: The first Block IIF satellite launched on 28 May 2010. It added the L5 civil signal and high-stability rubidium and cesium clocks. Block IIF launches ran from 2010 to 2016.
events.why: Extra signals let receivers cancel most of the delay caused by the upper atmosphere.

events.title: GLONASS is back to 24
events.text: GLONASS slipped in the 1990s after the Soviet collapse, and restoring it became a high priority in the early 2000s. Roscosmos said a launch in October 2011 brought the fleet back to full capability for the first time since 1996.
events.why: A system can decay without money, which is why GPS needs constant replacement launches.

events.title: The first Galileo satellite for service
events.text: On 21 October 2011 the first two operational Galileo satellites launched on a Soyuz rocket from Kourou, French Guiana. Galileo flies at about 23,222 km in three orbital planes.
events.why: Galileo sits higher than GPS, so a satellite stays in view a little longer.

events.title: BeiDou serves Asia and the Pacific
events.text: BeiDou began civilian positioning and messaging service in China and parts of the Asia-Pacific in December 2012. Sun Jiadong is listed by Wikipedia as chief designer of BeiDou-2.
events.why: It was the second stage of China's plan to go global.

events.title: India launches NavIC's seven satellites
events.text: IRNSS-1A launched on 1 July 2013 and IRNSS-1G, the seventh and last, on 28 April 2016. Three satellites are geostationary and four are inclined geosynchronous. NavIC covers India and a region up to 1,500 km beyond its borders.
events.why: A regional system can be much smaller and still serve a whole country.

events.title: Galileo starts serving the world
events.text: On 15 December 2016 the European Commission declared Galileo's Initial Services open, with 18 satellites in orbit. The Open Service is free. A search and rescue service cuts the wait to locate a distress beacon from up to three hours to about 10 minutes.
events.why: Phones could now use a second global system built on a civil design.

events.title: Japan's satellites hang over its cities
events.text: The first QZSS satellite, Michibiki, launched on 11 September 2010. The four-satellite system has been in service since November 2018. Its satellites follow inclined paths that trace a figure of eight, so at least one stays high over Japan.
events.why: Tall buildings block low satellites, so a high one overhead helps in a city street.

events.title: The first GPS III satellite
events.who: US Space Force and US Air Force
events.text: The first GPS III satellite launched in December 2018. GPS.gov says that in September 2007 the US decided to buy GPS III without the Selective Availability feature.
events.why: The old deliberate blur is gone from the design of the newest satellites.

events.title: BeiDou-3 goes global
events.text: On 31 July 2020 President Xi Jinping declared BeiDou-3 complete and in global service. It has 30 third-generation satellites: 24 in medium Earth orbit, 3 inclined geosynchronous and 3 geostationary. The last was launched in late June 2020.
events.why: The world now had four global systems, not one.

events.title: Galileo offers 20 cm accuracy
events.text: ESA says Galileo's High Accuracy Service, giving about 20 cm horizontal accuracy, was declared available on 24 January 2023. Surveyors have long used RTK, which uses carrier-wave measurements and a nearby base station for centimetre accuracy.
events.why: Centimetre-level accuracy is moving from surveying into everyday products.

events.title: Gladys West dies at 95
events.text: West died on 17 January 2026, aged 95. She was inducted into the US Air Force Space and Missile Pioneers Hall of Fame in 2018, retired from Dahlgren in 1998 after 42 years, and completed a doctorate in 2000.
events.why: A woman whose maths sat under every GPS fix was honoured late in life.

series.caption: Early satellites flew low and crossed the sky quickly. Later ones climbed to about 20,000 km so each stays in view for hours.

facts: Light travels about 300 m in a millionth of a second, so a receiver clock that is off by one microsecond would put you about 300 m out.
Satellite clocks tick about 38 microseconds a day faster than clocks on the ground. Left uncorrected, the error would grow by more than 11 km in a day.
Engineers set each satellite clock to run slightly slow before launch so it ticks at the right rate once it is in orbit.
A GPS satellite sends its data at only 50 bits per second, and the full message takes 750 seconds.
